projects.title: Langfuse Observability Dashboard
projects.summary: Air-gapped observability dashboard for Langfuse traces: a re-runnable fetch pipeline (traces, observations, sessions, scores) plus a single-file, dark-theme dashboard with KPIs, time-series, model breakdown and a trace drill-down. The ingestion broker's whitelist blocks data-plane reads (403), so the shipped build honestly renders a "no data — read blocked at broker" state with the 403 evidence recorded verbatim in the fetched JSON.
highlights: Idempotent fetch pipeline: atomic rewrites, page- and cursor-based pagination, ~5000-item caps per collection
Credentials from environment only; no secret ever printed or written to disk
Single-file dashboard, zero network requests, data embedded as a JS const so it opens over file://
Trace explorer drills into the observations parent/child tree with latency, usage and I/O previews
Verified broker behaviour endpoint by endpoint: health/projects OK, traces/observations/sessions/scores all 403 — failure recorded, nothing fabricated

projects.title: Model Quality Harness
projects.summary: Deterministic tool-calling reliability benchmark for local LLMs behind an OpenAI-compatible LiteLLM broker: a fixed 8-scenario suite, simulated tool execution, rule-by-rule scoring with no LLM judge, and a standalone HTML dashboard rendered from the real results JSON.
highlights: 8-scenario fixed suite: single-tool lookups, multi-constraint calls, two-step dependencies, and a retry scenario where the simulator rejects the first call
Deterministic judge only — schema-valid tool-call JSON, parameter accuracy under normalization, and success criteria like call_made / params_exact / param_absent / answer_contains
Tracks silent failures HTTP 200 hides: empty_content_turns, reasoning_burn_turns (finish_reason=length with content null), finish_reason per turn
Proved the broker response-cached identical request bodies (~0.01 s replays); cache-busting user stamps restored real latency distributions (min 0.83 s / med 1.31 s / max 3.72 s)
Broker outages are recorded as failures with the real HTTP error body, never papered over

projects.title: DuckDB MCP Server
projects.summary: Model Context Protocol server exposing 15 DuckDB database tools — query, schema, import/export, profiling, cross-database operations — over stdio JSON-RPC. Drives the DuckDB CLI binary via subprocess (no Python duckdb binding), and encodes 9 benchmark-proven best practices as tested utilities and SQL recipes.
highlights: 15 tools spanning query, DDL/DML, CSV/Parquet import-export, profiling, ATTACH-based cross-DB joins
CLI subprocess over the Python binding: no version drift, -json output parsed with recursive type coercion to int/float/bool/None
Multi-statement SQL via temp files and duckdb -f, dodging argument-length limits
9 benchmark-proven best practices as code (bulk insert via generate_series: 100K users in 27 ms; 3x100K cross-DB join in 8 ms; Parquet at ~27% of CSV size), each pinned by an integration test
Pitfall guard for the real DuckDB failure mode: IDENTITY/SERIAL fails, so auto-increment goes through CREATE SEQUENCE + nextval()

projects.title: Multi-MCP Orchestrator
projects.summary: Unified CLI frontend over six in-process MCP servers (DuckDB analytics, metrics, site audit, system telemetry, task management, wiki search), composed by direct Python imports instead of JSON-RPC, with a chained pipeline mode and DuckDB-backed trend queries.
highlights: Direct Python import of six MCP server modules bypasses stdio/JSON-RPC overhead for same-process composition
Single _call_tool dispatcher normalizes divergent handler return shapes (tuple-with-dict vs list-of-TextContent) behind asyncio.run wrapping
Chained pipeline actions: scan, find, tasks, wiki, db, trends run as one command
Documented integration pitfalls: import order after sys.path setup, _tool_manager._tools vs _tool_map, dispatcher registration order

posts.title: DuckDB is the analytics database your agent workflows needed
posts.summary: What a 14-benchmark suite says about wiring agents to DuckDB: 100K inserts in 27 ms, cross-database joins in 8 ms, Parquet at a quarter of CSV's size — and the one DDL feature that fails loudly when you least expect it.
posts.html:
When you build tools that let an LLM agent query data, the database choice stops being an architecture-slide decision and becomes a failure-mode decision: what happens when the model does something reasonable-sounding but slow, or generates DDL that quietly does not work. I benchmarked that question the slow way — a 14-benchmark suite behind the duckdb-mcp server, measuring everything from DDL speed to MCP round-trip overhead. The numbers argued for DuckDB, and the gotchas were worth the exercise by themselves.

The numbers that changed my defaults

All figures below come from the project's benchmark suite (test_benchmarks.py and the integration tests that pin each practice), run against DuckDB CLI 1.5.4+.

Bulk insert: generate_series, never INSERT VALUES. 100,000 users land in 27 ms via a select-from-generate_series. Hand the same task to a model's natural instinct — long INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...), (...) lists — and you are paying parse costs per statement, and the practice guide's rule of thumb is to stop generating them past a thousand rows anyway.

Parquet as the ingest format, not CSV. Parquet files came in around 27% of the equivalent CSV size, and read_parquet queries the file zero-copy without loading it into a database first. For agent pipelines this matters twice: files are what agents pass around, and smaller files mean fewer tokens spent on paths and less time on IO.

Cross-database joins are instant. Three attached databases of 100K rows each joined in 8 ms. One caveat that cost me an hour: ATTACH only works against file-backed databases, not :memory: — so anything doing cross-DB work needs temp files, which the server does for you.

Window functions scale flat-ish. ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, running sums and NTILE at 100K rows all landed in a uniform 6.9–7.5 ms band. The kind of analysis an agent is most likely to be asked for is exactly what columnar engines are boringly good at.

JSON output is affordable. The CLI's -json mode adds 9–15% overhead versus plain text. For machine-readable tool responses, that is a tax worth paying — but see the coercion post, because the JSON types need re-hydration.

The failure you will only find at runtime

Here is the one the documentation under-sells: on DuckDB v1.5.4, DEFAULT, UNIQUE, CHECK and FOREIGN KEY constraints all work fine. IDENTITY and SERIAL fail with Constraint not implemented!. Any model trained on Postgres-heavy corpora will generate SERIAL PRIMARY KEY on demand, all day, and every one of those calls dies.

The fix is not a prompt patch, it is a tool-level pattern:

CREATE SEQUENCE user_id_seq;
CREATE TABLE users (
  id BIGINT DEFAULT nextval('user_id_seq') PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT UNIQUE CHECK (email LIKE '%@%')
);

Auto-increment through CREATE SEQUENCE + nextval() works and keeps the IDs in the database, where they belong — the practice notes are blunt about it: never generate IDs in Python, use DuckDB-native bulk patterns. Because the MCP server exposes schema creation through recipes that already use the working pattern, the model never gets the chance to discover the failure at 3 a.m. on someone's pipeline.

Why this matters for agents specifically

An agent workflow is an unpredictable query generator with a budget. Three properties of DuckDB line up with that: it is a library-grade database that needs no server to administer (an agent can be handed a file path and be productive immediately), it is columnar and fast on exactly the analytical shapes models tend to write, and its failure modes are loud exceptions rather than silent plan degradations.

The benchmark suite is not an argument that DuckDB beats a warehouse for everything — 500K rows is not big data. It is an argument that for the agent-tooling niche — single-node files, sub-second interactive queries, Parquet in the middle, JSON out the other side — the boring choice is the database that lets your tools encode the three patterns that work and make the wrong ones impossible.

posts.title: MCP in production: what the spec doesn't tell you
posts.summary: Field notes from shipping a 15-tool DuckDB MCP server and a six-server orchestrator: stdio lifecycle quirks, argument-length walls, JSON type erosion, return-shape chaos, and why direct imports beat JSON-RPC in-process.
posts.html:
The MCP spec is short enough to read in an afternoon and vague enough to hide about a week of debugging in every one of its "implementations MAY" clauses. I shipped two projects that live on both sides of that vagueness: duckdb-mcp, a stdio MCP server exposing 15 DuckDB tools, and orchestrator, a CLI that composes six MCP servers in one process. Here is what the spec did not warn me about.

1. FastMCP is a toy; the low-level server is the job

FastMCP gets you a hello world in ten lines. The moment you need a tool router, structured error semantics, or control over the JSON-RPC lifecycle, you want the lower-level mcp.server.stdio API with an explicit Server instance. The DuckDB server ends up as three pieces: a TOOLS list of tool-definition objects with input schemas, a HANDLERS dict mapping tool names to async functions, and a call_tool router that dispatches by name. That separation costs you nothing and pays for itself the first time a tool needs to return a structured error instead of crashing the connection.

2. You will hit the argument-length wall

My first instinct for running SQL through the DuckDB CLI was duckdb -c "SELECT ...". Multi-statement scripts, or anything with bulk data, eventually dies on the OS argument-length limit. The pattern that holds: write the SQL to a temp file and run duckdb -f tmpfile.sql. Same for results: -json mode gives you structured output that you parse yourself. Which leads to the next one.

3. JSON over stdio erodes your types

DuckDB's -json output stringifies a lot of what you thought were numbers and booleans. If you hand that straight to a model, the model will learn that count looks like "42" and start emitting comparisons against strings. The server has a recursive _coerce_types() pass that walks parsed JSON and converts strings back to int, float, bool, and None. Every tool boundary where you serialize through the weakest format in the pipe needs a re-hydration step on the way back. Nobody tells you this in the protocol docs because the protocol has no types to lose — your data does.

4. Return shapes are a folklore, not a standard

When the orchestrator imports six MCP server modules directly (more on that below), I found their call_tool implementations do not agree on anything: one returns a tuple of (list_of_TextContent, dict) where the useful payload lives at index 1; the rest return a bare list of TextContent whose .text is a JSON string. The dispatcher is 15 lines of shape-sniffing. The spec describes what a wire response looks like, not what your in-process handler function returns, so every server you import is a small archaeology dig. Two more discoveries, filed under "why are these not in the README": tool listings live on _tool_manager._tools, not _tool_map, and server modules with top-level imports must be imported after sys.path is set up.

5. In-process, skip the wire entirely

JSON-RPC over stdio exists to cross a process boundary. When the consumer is your own Python CLI, that boundary is pure overhead — serialization, subprocess lifecycle, an event loop per server. The orchestrator imports the server modules directly and calls asyncio.run(server.call_tool(name, kwargs)). That collapses "run a code-quality scan, log the findings as tasks, write a wiki report, query the trend in DuckDB" from a distributed-systems problem into one command. The stdio transport stays where it belongs: for external clients like Claude Desktop or IDE integrations.

6. The server is where the lessons belong

The most useful thing duckdb-mcp does is not query execution — it is that nine benchmark-proven practices are encoded in the tools themselves: bulk insert via generate_series instead of INSERT VALUES, CREATE SEQUENCE instead of broken IDENTITY/SERIAL, Parquet-first ingest. The server stops the model from choosing the wrong pattern, which is worth more than any prompt that says "please prefer bulk inserts". Treat your MCP server as the place where operational knowledge becomes a tool constraint.

The spec covers the handshake. Everything above is the part you learn by having the thing fail at 2 a.m., and all of it is now a unit test.

posts.title: Building an eval harness that catches silent model regressions
posts.summary: How a deterministic, no-LLM-judge harness for tool-calling reliability caught three classes of failure that HTTP 200 hides: empty content turns, reasoning burn, and a response cache that was lying about latency.
posts.html:
Every team that ships an LLM feature eventually builds an eval harness, and every harness eventually answers the same question wrong: did the model succeed, or did the HTTP layer just return 200? This post is the methodology behind the harness I built for local models behind an OpenAI-compatible LiteLLM broker — eight scenarios, three models, two repetitions, and a scoring pass that never asks another model for its opinion.

The scenario suite is fixed and adversarial

The suite ships as eight JSON files. Each scenario defines an OpenAI function schema, a user prompt, simulated tool implementations, and success criteria. The scenarios escalate deliberately:

  • weather_tokyo — one tool call, final answer must cite the tool's value.

  • table_booking — argument extraction: "eight people" and "7:30 PM" must arrive as party_size: 8 and 19:30.

  • pizza_distractor — an expired coupon in context that must not appear in the call (param_absent).

  • inventory_then_reserve — a two-step dependency: query the catalog, take the SKU from the tool result, reserve with it.

  • fx_conversion_retry — the first call uses non-ISO currency names and the simulator rejects it; the model must retry with EUR/USD. The retry scenario is the one that separates models. A single-shot accuracy metric says nothing about whether a model can consume a tool error and recover, which is most of what agent loops actually do.

Deterministic judging, on purpose

There is no LLM-as-judge anywhere in the pipeline. Each emitted tool call is validated against the scenario's function schema — no missing required keys, no extras, no mistyped params — and parameter accuracy is checked under normalization (numbers compared as floats, strings trimmed and case-insensitive). The final answer is graded with criteria kinds like:

{
  "kind": "params_exact_any",
  "tool": "convert_currency",
  "params": { "from": "EUR", "to": "USD" }
}

A fluent-but-wrong answer passes only if it actually states the expected values (answer_contains matches case-insensitively and tolerates thousands separators, so 1,301.04 matches 1301.04). Yes, substring checks are dull. They are also reproducible, which is the property an eval needs when its whole job is telling you that Tuesday's deploy made Thursday worse.

What HTTP 200 hides

Three real findings, all from logging one field deeper than the status code.

Empty content turns. A turn can return 200 with content: null. The harness records empty_content_turns per scenario; a model that "completed" without ever producing usable content now fails loudly instead of silently.

Reasoning burn. One of the tested models is a reasoning model served by vLLM. With a small max_tokens the entire output budget disappears into reasoning_content while content stays null and finish_reason reads length. That combination — finish_reason=length plus empty content plus non-zero reasoning — is scored as a distinct failure mode (reasoning_burn_turns), and scoring calls get max_tokens=2048 precisely to avoid measuring it as model incompetence when it is really a sampling-budget artifact.

The cache that flattered everyone. The broker response-caches identical request bodies. Sending the same JSON body twice returned the cached completion in ~0.01 s with the same id — which made rep-to-rep variance look near zero and latency look phenomenal. Proof: a repeated body came back in 0.01 s versus ~1.4 s for a distinct one. The fix is one field: every request gets a unique user: mqh-<uuid> stamp to bust the cache. After the fix the same model's per-turn latency showed a real distribution — min 0.83 s, median 1.31 s, max 3.72 s — where before it showed a flat line that was never real.

Outages are data, not footnotes

During one re-run, two of the three models were down at the broker: one returned a LiteLLM 404 (the upstream model does not exist), the other a 500 connection error. Both ran anyway and both were recorded as failures with the real HTTP error bodies attached, and the dashboard shows that honestly rather than silently shrinking the comparison to the one live model. 4xx responses fail fast; only timeout/429/5xx get the single retry. A harness that quietly drops unavailable models is not an eval, it is marketing.

The whole thing is Python 3.13 stdlib only — no pip, no framework, ~5–10 minutes for a full run, and a standalone vanilla-JS dashboard rendered from the results JSON. The point of an eval harness is not sophistication. It is that the same input gives you the same number twice, so the day the number moves, you can believe it.
